entries.title: Lost City Hydrothermal Field
paragraphs: The Lost City Hydrothermal Field sits on the southern summit of the Atlantis Massif, a dome-shaped mountain of mantle rock exposed on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge near 30°N. Unlike the famous 'black smoker' vents that run on volcanic heat, Lost City is powered by serpentinization: seawater reacting with olivine-rich mantle rock, producing heat, hydrogen and methane without any magma nearby.

The field was found on 4 December 2000 by scientists diving in DSV Alvin with the robotic camera sled ArgoII, working from the research vessel Atlantis. Its towering white carbonate chimneys, some over 60 m tall, made it one of the most striking hydrothermal discoveries ever made.

The vent fluid is warm, around 40–90 °C, and strongly alkaline. It emerges clear rather than carrying the dark mineral particles of a black smoker. Calcium carbonate and brucite build the white towers where this fluid meets seawater.

NOAA’s 2005 expedition described a field covering about 60,000 square metres. Individual chimneys are smaller than the terrain grid can resolve; their positions here follow nearby terrain in the documented depth range.

entries.title: Poseidon, the tallest tower
paragraphs: Poseidon is a composite carbonate edifice about 60 m tall and 100 m across. Its adjoining towers, spires and flanges grow as warm vent fluid mixes with cold seawater and deposits minerals.

Uranium-thorium dating of carbonate samples from across Lost City gives ages up to about 120,000 years. These samples record the field’s long history; they do not date the entire active Poseidon tower.

Because it needs only olivine rock and liquid water, serpentinization like this could in principle happen anywhere those two things meet -- including on icy moons such as Europa or Enceladus, which is one reason Lost City is studied as a possible model for life beyond Earth.

facts.label: Built from
facts.value: calcium carbonate, precipitated from alkaline vent fluid

entries.title: Beehive
paragraphs: Beehive was a small, roughly 1 m high vent on Poseidon's flank. It released some of the hottest fluid measured at Lost City, about 91 degC during earlier surveys. Later researchers reported that the chimney itself was gone by their 2018 visit, although fluid still vented from its former opening.
Its marker here is offset from Poseidon so you can scan it separately.

facts.label: Historical height
facts.value: about 1 m; structure absent in 2018 survey

entries.title: IMAX Tower
paragraphs: IMAX is a parasitic chimney and flange on Poseidon's north face, built as warm, alkaline vent fluid mixed with seawater and deposited carbonate minerals. A 2005 expedition account described the chimney as about 8 m tall; a later detailed geologic survey described a roughly 30 m multipronged structure. Those measurements may refer to different parts of the growing complex.
Its perch on Poseidon's flank makes it an easy stop right after the main tower, without a long swim across the field.

facts.label: Published heights
facts.value: about 8 m (2005 account); roughly 30 m (2016 survey)

entries.title: Microbial life on the chimneys
paragraphs: Lost City's chimneys are coated inside and out with thick biofilms of archaea and bacteria that live on the vent's own chemistry: hydrogen and methane, produced abiotically by the serpentinization reaction, with almost no help from sunlight or photosynthesis at all. A group of archaea related to the order Methanosarcinales dominates the warmest, most active surfaces.

Larger animals are scarce compared with a black-smoker field: there are no tubeworms or giant clams here, the signature animals of sulfide vents. Instead, small corals, snails, bivalves, worms and crustaceans graze on the microbial mats and on each other.

This POI sits near a real cluster of OBIS occurrence records from a 2003 International Census of Marine Microbes survey of the field -- almost entirely archaea and bacteria identified from DNA, with no reported collection depth.

facts.label: Large fauna
facts.value: small corals, snails, bivalves, polychaetes, amphipods, ostracods -- no tubeworms or vent clams

entries.title: The Atlantis Massif summit
paragraphs: The Atlantis Massif is an oceanic core complex: a dome of deep mantle and lower-crust rock, normally buried many kilometres down, exposed at the seafloor by a long-lived detachment fault that slides one tectonic block up and over another. Its summit, the shallowest point in this tile at 724 m, sits about 15 km from the main Mid-Atlantic Ridge spreading axis -- unusually far for hydrothermal activity, another sign that Lost City is not driven by fresh volcanic heat like a ridge-axis black smoker field.
This is the actual shallowest terrain sampled anywhere in this tile.

entries.title: A coordinate discrepancy
paragraphs: The Atlantis Massif’s south wall falls steeply below the carbonate terrace. At this scan point the terrain is about 1,332 m deep, more than 500 m below the main vent field.
The catalog’s rounded position lands on this wall. The dive’s tower markers lie farther north, where the terrain matches Lost City’s documented 750–900 m depth range.

facts.label: Cause
facts.value: arc-minute-rounded published coordinate on steep terrain
